headline: RBA holds rates steady giving mortgage holders a breather, while GXAI takes a nasty 7.6% hit on the ASX today.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: The biggest mover in your portfolio today — down 7.6% at the close. No specific news triggered this drop, but AI-themed ETFs have been volatile lately as markets digest whether AI spending translates to profits. With the fund already down 11.4% on your total investment, this one needs watching.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft had a strong night last night on the NASDAQ, jumping 3% to $384.28 USD. No single headline drove it but the broader market mood around AI and cloud is doing MSFT favours right now — it's been one of the loudest voices in the AI spending story. Still down 13.3% overall on your investment though.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google ticked up 1.3% last night to $357.89 USD — a solid session. The stock is now up 16.4% on your total investment. Google's Gemini AI pricing cuts (it's the only major AI service cutting prices right now) may be helping sentiment around its competitiveness.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: A small positive day for Pilbara, edging up 0.4% to $5.13 at today's ASX close. Analysts are asking whether PLS can lead a lithium recovery — the lithium battery market is forecast to grow strongly toward 2035 on grid-scale energy storage demand. Still down 23.9% on your total investment though, so this is a slow grind back.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two was basically flat last night, up just 0.1% to $250.32. The GTA 6 buzz continues but it's being clouded by stories about Rockstar developers complaining about pay inequity and 'crunch' culture — the kind of PR noise that doesn't usually move the stock but is worth watching if it escalates.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: Barely moved today — up 0.04% to $535.53. This tracks the entire US share market, and with the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both dipping slightly last night, the ASX-listed version is holding steady on the back of yesterday's US close.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: Effectively flat today, down just 2 cents to $75.78. This is a broad 'set and forget' fund — no specific news, just gentle background noise. It's up 0.5% on your total investment, doing its job quietly.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Almost unchanged today at $94.94, down 3 cents. Emerging markets have been quiet. With Chinese AI models closing the gap on US rivals (see AI section), there's a long-term tailwind for the emerging market tech story, but nothing moving the needle today.

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy ETF
movers.note: FUEL had a rough session today, dropping 2.3% to $7.67. Crude oil (WTI) fell 0.6% last night to $68.16 USD a barrel, dragging energy stocks lower globally. Oil has been soft lately as OPEC supply remains elevated and demand concerns linger — that's bad news for an energy-focused ETF.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — sharp 7.6% drop today
watch_today.detail: Your Global X AI ETF fell 7.57% in today's session to $16.73, and is now down 11.4% on your total investment of $297. There's no single news catalyst in today's data — this looks like a sector-wide pullback in AI-themed stocks. At this level it's worth reviewing whether the thesis still holds. No reason to panic-sell, but worth watching if it keeps sliding.

watch_today.title: MSFT surged 3% last night — a bright spot
watch_today.detail: Microsoft jumped $11.26 to $384.28 USD last night, its best session in a while. The AI and cloud narrative is firmly behind it. Your position is still down 13.3% overall, so this is a welcome recovery move. Hold and let it run — no reason to sell into strength.

watch_today.title: RBA holds rates — good news for your overall financial picture
watch_today.detail: The Reserve Bank of Australia left interest rates on hold today, giving mortgage holders a breather. This should support consumer spending and keep the ASX on a stable footing. However, at least one economist is warning that the Federal Budget's stimulus effect on housing could push inflation back up, meaning further cuts might be delayed. Watch for the next RBA meeting for any change in tone.

watch_today.title: FUEL.AX sliding with oil prices
watch_today.detail: Your energy ETF dropped 2.3% today as crude oil sits at $68.16/barrel — near recent lows. If oil keeps softening (OPEC supply is elevated and global demand is uncertain), FUEL could see further pressure. No urgent action needed but this is a holding to keep an eye on.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — tiny green day, long road back
watch_today.detail: Pilbara crept up 0.4% today to $5.13, but you're still sitting on a 23.9% loss on this position. Multiple analyst pieces this week are asking whether PLS can lead a lithium recovery. Long-term lithium battery demand looks solid toward 2035, but the near-term market is still soft. Hold unless your conviction has changed.

watch_today.title: GTA 6 developer controversy — watch TTWO
watch_today.detail: Rockstar Games (owned by Take-Two, your TTWO holding) is facing media scrutiny over alleged worker pay inequity, crunch culture, and bonuses being used as control mechanisms. This PR headwind could weigh on sentiment as GTA 6's release approaches. The stock was flat last night — it hasn't bitten yet, but keep an eye on it.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 crept up just 0.02% today to 8,724 — essentially flat, with the RBA rate hold giving markets comfort but not excitement. Last night on Wall Street, both the S&P 500 (-0.22%) and the NASDAQ (-0.66%) slipped modestly. Gold is nudging higher at $4,084 USD/oz, the Aussie dollar is steady at 69.1 US cents, and oil is soft at $68.16/barrel.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Barely moved today — the RBA hold was expected so markets didn't react dramatically.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Slight dip last night — nothing alarming, just a bit of profit-taking after recent highs.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech stocks dipped last night despite MSFT and GOOG having good sessions individually.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil slipping — elevated OPEC supply and soft demand keeping prices under pressure.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold edging higher — investors still want a safe haven amid uncertainty.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar is holding steady — the rate hold didn't spook currency markets.

politics.summary: The RBA's decision to hold interest rates dominated domestic news today. Separately, the federal government is moving to ban gambling influencers and tighten advertising laws, while a proposed $50 billion data centre deal is stirring up debate about AI copyright and environmental impact.

stories.title: RBA holds interest rates — relief for borrowers, but warnings remain
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank left interest rates unchanged at its July meeting, giving mortgage holders a break from rate rises. However, at least one economist is warning that positive economic signals — including the government's budget stimulus flowing through — could push inflation back up and delay any rate cuts. Separately, ABC News analysis suggests today's homeowners are actually doing it tougher than in the era of 17% interest rates, because house prices are so much higher relative to incomes. The RBA also flagged that the federal budget is influencing the housing market in ways that complicate its inflation fight.

stories.title: Labor moves to ban gambling influencers
stories.why_it_matters: The federal government is introducing legislation to ban influencers from promoting gambling products — a crackdown aimed squarely at social media personalities who effectively advertise betting apps to young audiences. The Greens are pushing for even tougher reforms and have secured a Senate inquiry. This is part of a broader gambling advertising reform push that's been building for two years. If you follow any sport, you'll notice how pervasive gambling ads have become — this is the government's attempt to pull back on that.

stories.title: Greens slam $50bn data centre proposal as 'dirty deal' — AI copyright debate erupts
stories.why_it_matters: Greens Senator David Pocock has labelled a proposed $50 billion data centre development the 'ultimate dirty deal,' raising concerns about its energy footprint and the lack of environmental scrutiny. At the same time, Australian artists and creatives are sounding the alarm about AI companies training their models on copyrighted work without permission or payment. Both issues are part of a growing national debate about how Australia handles the AI infrastructure boom — and whether it comes at too high a cost to the environment and creative industries.

ai.summary: Big AI news this week: Anthropic launched Claude Sonnet 5, Chinese AI models are closing the gap on US leaders, the US government has lifted restrictions on Anthropic's most powerful models, and the UN is warning that AI is advancing faster than regulators can keep up. Meanwhile, courts are split on whether training AI on copyrighted data is legal.

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Sonnet 5
stories.why_it_matters: Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5 this week — its latest mid-tier AI model. This sits between the lightweight Haiku and the flagship Opus models, meaning it's designed to be fast, affordable, and capable for everyday tasks like coding, writing, and analysis. If you use Claude for work, this is the version you're most likely to be using day-to-day. The launch comes as a pricing war heats up — Google's Gemini is currently the only major AI service actually cutting prices, while most others (including Anthropic) are holding steady or adding new tiers.

stories.title: US lifts restrictions on Anthropic's powerful AI models Fable and Mythos
stories.why_it_matters: The White House has removed export and usage restrictions on Anthropic's two most powerful AI models — called Fable and Mythos — which are described as 'cyber-capable,' meaning they can assist with complex cybersecurity tasks. In response to this deregulation, Anthropic itself is now lobbying for AI regulation, arguing that some guardrails are needed. This is a notable role reversal: usually it's governments pushing for rules and companies pushing back. It signals just how powerful these models are becoming.

stories.title: Chinese AI models close the gap with Anthropic and OpenAI
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese AI companies are rapidly catching up to Anthropic and OpenAI according to new benchmarks reported by the New York Times. This matters because it challenges the assumption that US AI firms have an unassailable lead. For investors in US tech (like your GOOG and MSFT holdings), increased competition from Chinese models could eventually pressure margins and market share — particularly in Asia. It also complicates the geopolitical picture around AI chip export restrictions.

stories.title: UN warns AI advancing faster than regulation can keep up
stories.why_it_matters: UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged world governments not to delay AI regulation, warning that the technology is advancing faster than both scientific understanding and the law. He called for international cooperation on AI safety frameworks. This follows similar warnings from Anthropic this week. For everyday Australians, the practical implication is that AI tools are already being used in hiring, healthcare, and financial services — often without clear rules about how.

stories.title: Courts split on whether training AI on copyright is legal
stories.why_it_matters: US courts are currently split on whether it's legal for AI companies to train their models using copyrighted books, articles, and artwork without paying the creators. Some courts have ruled it falls under 'fair use' (a legal doctrine that allows limited use of copyrighted work without permission), while others have sided with creators. This legal uncertainty has a direct impact on companies like Google and Microsoft who have massive AI training operations — a definitive ruling against them could force costly changes to how these models are built.

sport.summary: NRL Round 18 kicks off tomorrow night. Wimbledon is producing drama — Nick Kyrgios is out and faces a fine, while a young Aussie stunned Serena Williams. The NRL is also reportedly closing in on a monster $5.3 billion TV rights deal, and the Broncos may be losing a giant prop to the NFL.

stories.title: Kyrgios crashes out of Wimbledon, faces fine for 'I don't care' attitude
stories.why_it_matters: Nick Kyrgios has been eliminated from Wimbledon and is reportedly facing a hefty fine for his conduct during his exit. His 'I don't care' comments post-match drew widespread criticism from the tennis world. Meanwhile, Alex de Minaur is one of just two Australian men to progress to the second round, keeping Aussie hopes alive at the All England Club.

stories.title: Young Aussie stuns Serena Williams in Wimbledon comeback
stories.why_it_matters: Serena Williams' highly anticipated Wimbledon comeback has been derailed by a young Australian player. The defeat sparked controversy after Serena's post-match behaviour was slammed by the tennis world — reports say she 'didn't need to act that way at Wimbledon.' The Australian Open final rematch is also headlining Day 3 of the tournament, adding to the drama in London.

stories.title: NRL reportedly closing in on $5.3 billion TV rights deal
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL is reportedly on the verge of signing a new television rights deal worth $5.3 billion — a monster agreement that would massively boost the league's finances for years to come. If confirmed, this would be one of the largest sports broadcast deals in Australian history and would flow through to player payments, club funding, and expansion ambitions. No timeframe was confirmed in the report.

stories.title: Broncos giant prop set for NFL shot — future of fellow prop 'uncertain'
stories.why_it_matters: A Brisbane Broncos giant prop is reportedly being courted by an NFL franchise — a rare crossover move that would see an elite NRL forward try his luck in American football. A teammate's future at the club is also described as 'uncertain,' adding to the off-season roster uncertainty at Red Hill. Round 18 kicks off tomorrow night with Broncos hosting the Sharks at Suncorp Stadium at 7:35pm.

stories.title: NRL Round 18 teams: Tigers blow, Eels make big halves call
stories.why_it_matters: Wests Tigers have copped a blow ahead of their Round 18 clash with St George Illawarra on Saturday — details of the injury weren't available in the article text but the Fox Sports teams analysis flags a 'silver lining.' The Eels have made a significant halves combination call ahead of their Sunday clash against the Sea Eagles at CommBank Stadium. Round 18 also features Panthers vs Rabbitohs tomorrow night at 8pm — seven clubs are on the bye including the Bulldogs, Cowboys, Raiders, Roosters, Storm, Titans, and Warriors.
